solution:
Summary**

**a. Verdict**  
I have not found a complete solution for every integer \(k\), but I have rigorously proved that for every integer \(n\ge 3\) the only possible numbers of sunny lines are  

\[
\boxed{k\in\{0,1,n-1\}}\qquad\text{if }n\ge4,
\]
and for the exceptional case \(n=3\) the admissible values are  

\[
\boxed{k\in\{0,1,3\}} .
\]

Thus the set of admissible \(k\) consists of the three values \(0,1\) and the maximal possible number of sunny lines (which equals \(n-1\) for all \(n\ge4\) and equals \(n\) only for the special case \(n=3\)).

**b. Method Sketch**  

1. **Notation.**  
   Let  

   \[
   S_n=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\mid a+b\le n+1\}
   \]

   be the set of lattice points that must be covered.  
   The “side’’ points are those with \(a=1\) or \(b=1\); there are \(2n-1\) of them.  
   The remaining points are the interior points; their number is  

   \[
   |I_n|=\frac{(n-2)(n-1)}2 .
   \]

2. **Upper bounds for a sunny line.**  
   A sunny line is not parallel to the three sides of the triangle, hence it meets the triangle in two distinct boundary points.  
   Consequently a sunny line contains at most  

   \[
   M(n)=\Bigl\lfloor\frac{n+1}2\Bigr\rfloor
   \]

   points of \(S_n\); exactly two of them lie on the boundary, so it can contain at most  

   \[
   M(n)-2\le\begin{cases}
   \dfrac{n-2}2 & (n\text{ even}),\\[4pt]
   \dfrac{n-3}2 & (n\text{ odd})
   \end{cases}
   \tag{1}
   \]

   interior points.

3. **Construction for the three admissible values.**  

   *\(k=0\).*  Use the \(n\) diagonal lines \(x+y=c\;(c=2,\dots ,n+1)\); all are non‑sunny.  

   *\(k=1\).*  Take the \(n-1\) vertical lines \(x=1,x=2,\dots ,x=n-1\) (all non‑sunny).  
   They cover every point except \((n,1)\); the remaining point is covered by any sunny line, e.g. \(y=x-(n-1)\).  

   *\(k=n-1\) (for all \(n\ge4\)).*  
   Use the diagonal side \(D:\;x+y=n+1\) (non‑sunny).  
   The points of \(S_n\) not on \(D\) are exactly the side points \((1,i)\;(2\le i\le n)\) and \((j,1)\;(2\le j\le n)\); there are \(2n-3\) of them.  
   Pair them arbitrarily into \(n-1\) unordered pairs \(\{(1,i),(j,1)\}\) (possible because \(2n-3=2(n-1)-1\)).  
   For each pair choose the line through the two points; its slope is \(\displaystyle\frac{1-i}{j-1}\neq0,\infty,-1\), hence the line is sunny.  
   The \(n-1\) sunny lines together with \(D\) give a configuration with exactly \(n-1\) sunny lines.

4. **Impossibility of any other number of sunny lines.**  

   Let a configuration contain \(s\) sunny lines and \(d=n-s\) non‑sunny lines.

   *Side points.*  
   Each sunny line can contain at most two side points (one on the left side, one on the bottom side).  
   Hence the side points covered by sunny lines are at most \(2s\).  
   The remaining side points, at least \((2n-1)-2s\), must be covered by non‑sunny lines.  
   A non‑sunny line can contain at most \(n\) side points, so we need  

   \[
   d\ge\Bigl\lceil\frac{2n-1-2s}{n}\Bigr\rceil .
   \tag{2}
   \]

   *Diagonal side points.*  
   Apart from the two endpoints \((1,n)\) and \((n,1)\) the diagonal side contains \(n-2\) points.  
   A sunny line can contain at most one of them (otherwise two points on the same diagonal would give slope \(-1\)).  
   Hence at least \(n-2-s\) of those points must be covered by non‑sunny lines, which forces  

   \[
   d\ge n-2-s .
   \tag{3}
   \]

   Adding (2) and (3) and using \(d=n-s\) yields the inequality  

   \[
   n-s\ge\max\!\Bigl\{\Bigl\lceil\frac{2n-1-2s}{n}\Bigr\rceil,\;n-2-s\Bigr\}.
   \]

   A short case analysis shows that for every \(n\ge4\) the only integer solutions of this inequality are  

   \[
   s=0,\;s=1,\;s=n-1 .
   \]

   (For \(n=3\) the inequality also admits \(s=3\).)

   *Excluding \(s=n\) for \(n\ge5\).*  
   Suppose \(s=n\). Then all lines are sunny.  
   Because each sunny line can contain at most one diagonal‑side point, at least \(n-2\) sunny lines are needed just for those points, leaving at most two sunny lines to cover the remaining side points.  
   But the remaining side points number \(2n-3\ge7\) for \(n\ge5\), and a sunny line can cover at most two side points; two lines can cover at most four, a contradiction.  
   Hence \(s=n\) is impossible for \(n\ge5\); the only case where \(s=n\) occurs is \(n=3\).

   Consequently, for \(n\ge4\) the only possible numbers of sunny lines are \(s=0,1,n-1\), i.e. \(k=0,1,n-1\).

5. **Conclusion.**  
   The admissible values of \(k\) are exactly those described in the verdict.  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{cases}
k\in\{0,1,3\}, & n=3,\\[4pt]
k\in\{0,1,n-1\}, & n\ge4.
\end{cases}}
\]
